outcome: Since 26 January 2024 nothing has settled or moved the planar constant F(Q²): its bounds remain 1/λ ≈ 0.1179 ≤ F(Q²) ≤ 1/4 − 1/384 ≈ 0.2474 (Bereg–Dumitrescu–Jiang, 2008), which a 2026 survey co-written by a BDJ author restates as current and lists as open, with F(Q²) < 1/4 since Ajtai (1973); the in-window items are a 2025 asymptotic for cubes that gives no planar number, that 2026 survey, and a 2026 paper on equal-size copies and balls, and no AI system is credited with any step.
problem_asks: Unpacking the statement from its wording alone: (a) for every finite family of axis-parallel squares in the plane whose union has area 1, take the largest total area of a pairwise disjoint subfamily; (b) the statement asks how small this quantity can be in the worst case, i.e. the infimum over all such families, which is the optimal constant F(Q²). The parts this requires are: (i) the exact value of that infimum; (ii) the guarantee side, a constant c such that every such family has a disjoint subfamily covering at least c of the union area, with the best such c; (iii) the extremal side, families showing that no larger guarantee holds. The statement allows squares of arbitrary and mutually different sizes; it names no equal-size restriction, no number of sizes, and no shape other than squares in the plane. It does not assert the conjectured value 1/4; it asks for the value.

events.what_happened: Tibor Radó, in the note 'Sur un problème relatif à un théorème de Vitali' (Fundamenta Mathematicae 11, 1928, pp. 228–229), proves the one-dimensional statement (every cover of the unit interval has disjoint subintervals of total length at least 1/2, sharp) and in the same paper, per the Xie–Ge introduction, proves the planar constant is at least 1/9 and conjectures it equals 1/4. Dall'Ara (2025) and the 2026 survey place the origin in a 1927 letter from Radó to Sierpiński; the public written argument is the 1928 note. I did not open the Fundamenta note itself; the 1/9 and the 1/4 conjecture come from Wikipedia and from the Xie–Ge introduction.
events.delivers: For squares of arbitrary sizes: every finite axis-parallel square family of union area 1 has a pairwise disjoint subfamily covering at least 1/9 of the union area. The 1/4 is a conjecture, not a delivered result.
events.remains: The exact value of F(Q²); the upper side; whether 1/4 is the value (later shown false for mixed sizes by Ajtai 1973, see that event).

checked_by.qualification: Editorial refereeing of the period; referees not identified in sources

events.direction: Guarantee direction: the answer to 'how small' is at least 1/9. It does not decide the exact value and does not cut against any stated claim.
events.object: The 2026 survey (Section 2) says a collection of squares in its Fig. 1 (right) shows the constant cannot be larger than 1/4. I did not see the figure, so the configuration is not described here, and I did not verify that the 1928 note contains it.

events.what_happened: Wikipedia states that the 1/4 conjecture was proved for equal squares, independently, by A. Sokolin (1940, Proc. USSR Acad. Sci. 26, pp. 871–872), R. Rado, and V. A. Zalgaller (1960, Matematicheskoe Prosveshchenie, 'Remarks on Rado's problem'). The year is taken from Wikipedia's reference list; I did not open these papers, and Wikipedia does not say which author proved what. The 2026 survey describes Sokolin differently: it says Sokolin recalled Radó's conjecture and generalised it to F(Q^d) = 2^-d in every dimension, i.e. as a conjecture, not a proof for equal squares. The two sources conflict and I have not resolved it.
events.delivers: Restricted to families of equal (same-size) axis-parallel squares: every such family has a disjoint subfamily covering at least 1/4 of the union area, and 1/4 is sharp for that restriction.
events.remains: Every family with unequal sizes, which is the bullet's problem as stated; so the exact general value remains open.

checked_by.who: A. Sokolin (1940); R. Rado and V. A. Zalgaller (1960)
checked_by.qualification: Authors working on this exact problem, per Wikipedia
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the equal-square result, per Wikipedia's reference list; not verified in primary text

events.doubts: Attribution conflict: Wikipedia credits Sokolin with the equal-square proof; the 2026 survey describes Sokolin's contribution as the dimension-d conjecture F(Q^d) = 2^-d. Primary papers not read.
events.direction: Guarantee at 1/4, for the equal-size restriction only. It agrees with the conjectured 1/4 for that restriction and does not bear on mixed sizes.

events.what_happened: Miklós Ajtai, 'The solution of a problem of T. Radó' (Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. 21, 1973, pp. 61–63, per Wikipedia), gives a finite family of axis-parallel squares of two different sizes in which every pairwise disjoint subfamily covers less than 1/4 of the total covered area. Wikipedia gives the bound as 1/4 − 1/1728 ≈ 0.2494; the 2026 survey states only F(Q²) < 1/4 and calls this a disproof of the two-dimensional conjecture. Dall'Ara (2025) describes the construction as an explicit finite collection of axis-parallel squares in the plane with every disjoint subcollection occupying a fraction below 1/4. I did not open Ajtai's paper.
events.delivers: For mixed-size families: a specific family for which the best disjoint subfamily covers at most 1/4 − 1/1728 of the union (Wikipedia figure), hence F(Q²) < 1/4. A single explicit two-size counterexample to the conjectured 1/4.
events.remains: The exact value of F(Q²); the lower bound side; the window between the best known lower and upper bounds.

checked_by.who: Bulletin de l'Académie Polonaise des Sciences (journal of record)
checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal of the period; referees not identified

events.direction: Cuts against the conjectured 1/4 for mixed sizes: the constant is strictly below 1/4. It does not settle the value.
events.object: An explicit finite family of axis-parallel squares in the plane, of two different sizes, such that every pairwise disjoint subfamily covers less than 1/4 of the union area; Wikipedia gives the maximum fraction as 1/4 − 1/1728 ≈ 0.2494. The construction is explicit, not a non-constructive existence proof. I did not read the construction itself.

events.what_happened: Sergey Bereg, Adrian Dumitrescu and Minghui Jiang, 'On covering problems of Rado' (SWAT 2008; full version Algorithmica 57(3), 538–561, 2010, DOI 10.1007/s00453-009-9298-z). Their refinement of Ajtai's construction (a reduced two-size system, replicated as a periodic plane tiling, per the Bridges exhibit and the survey) gives F(Q²) ≤ 1/4 − 1/384 ≈ 0.2474. The 2026 survey attributes to them the lower bound F(Q²) ≥ 1/λ_square ≈ 1/8.4797 ≈ 0.1179, and their general-dimension lower bound F(Q^d) ≥ (3^d − 1/2 + o(1))⁻¹ (survey, Theorem 1 of [3]); at d = 2 that expression is about 1/8.5, consistent with the square-specific figure. Wikipedia gives the same two numbers. The MARDI record lists the SWAT publication as 15 July 2008. I could not read the Springer pages (redirect to a login page).
events.revisions: SWAT 2008 announcement; full version Algorithmica 57(3) 2010 (per MARDI record and Wikipedia). Full-version content not checked against the conference text.
events.delivers: For mixed-size axis-parallel square families: the best guaranteed disjoint fraction lies between about 0.1179 and 1/4 − 1/384 ≈ 0.2474, both non-sharp. The lower bound holds for all families; the upper bound is an explicit counterexample family. Neither bound is sharp.
events.remains: The exact value of F(Q²). The 2026 survey lists both 'Can these bounds be improved?' questions as open.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal; referees not named publicly
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the full version (2010), per the MARDI record and Wikipedia citation

checked_by.who: Gian Maria Dall'Ara and Adrian Dumitrescu (2026 semi-survey)
checked_by.qualification: Dumitrescu is the second named author of the BDJ paper, so this is not an independent check
checked_by.what_they_did: Restated the 1/λ_square and 1/4 − 1/384 bounds as the current state of the art and listed their improvement as open

events.direction: Moves both sides of F(Q²) relative to the earlier state: lower bound to about 0.1179 from Radó's 1/9; upper bound to 1/4 − 1/384 from Ajtai's 1/4 − 1/1728. Neither side is sharp, so the value is not settled.
events.object: A periodic tiling of the plane by a composite tile built from a reduced two-size square system; every pairwise disjoint subfamily covers at most 1/4 − 1/384 of the total union area (Bridges exhibit page and survey Section 5, not read in primary text). The construction is explicit, not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: R. Rado, 'Some covering theorems (I)' (Proc. London Math. Soc. 51, 1949, pp. 232–264, per Wikipedia's reference list), treats the analogous constant for general convex shapes. Wikipedia reports that for a triangle f(X) = 1/6 exactly, and for a centrally symmetric hexagon f(X) = 1/4. This is a different shape from a square and does not concern squares; I did not open the paper.
events.delivers: For triangles and centrally symmetric hexagons only (per Wikipedia): exact values 1/6 and 1/4 of the analogous constant. Restricted to those shapes.
events.remains: Everything for squares; the squares constant is not addressed.
events.direction: Neighbouring problem (other convex shapes). No direct bearing on the square constant.

events.what_happened: Peter Brass, Ferran Hurtado, Benjamin Lafreniere and Anna Lubiw, 'A Lower Bound on the Area of a 3-Coloured Disk Packing' (arXiv:0804.1173, cs.CG, submitted 8 April 2008). For unit disks, the abstract restates Rado's disk conjecture of 1/4 and his proved 1/4.41. For a 3-coloured variant (a subset that is 3-colourable with same-colour disks disjoint), they prove 1/2.09 of the union area, conjecture 1/1.41, and give an O(n²) algorithm achieving 1/2.77. A Waterloo thesis record 'Packing Unit Disks' appears in search results; not opened.
events.delivers: For unit disks with a 3-colouring condition: a guaranteed fraction 1/2.09 of the union area. Scope: disks, not squares; the colouring condition is an added restriction.
events.remains: The square constant F(Q²), and for disks the unrestricted constant (not established by this paper).
events.direction: Neighbouring problem (unit disks, 3-coloured variant). It bears on the square problem only by analogy.

events.what_happened: Gian Maria Dall'Ara, 'On the best constant in the finitary Vitali covering lemma for high dimensional cubes' (arXiv:2510.06817, math.CA, submitted 8 October 2025, one version listed). Defines Γ_d as the best constant for axis-parallel cubes in R^d (for d = 2, squares, which is F(Q²)). Proves Γ_d ≥ c·2^-d/(d log d) for an absolute constant c > 0 in every dimension (Theorem 1.3; constant can be taken as about e^(−1−(log log d)/log d+O(1/log d))). States that Radó's conjecture on the two-dimensional constant was disproved by Ajtai in 1973. Gives no numerical value for Γ_2, and says its argument is worse than Vitali's 3^-d bound for d ≤ 13, so it gives no improvement at d = 2. The abstract claims it answers Croft–Falconer–Guy problem D6.
events.revisions: v1 only (8 Oct 2025), per arXiv abstract page as summarised
events.delivers: For cubes in every dimension d: the best constant Γ_d is at least c·2^-d/(d log d). The paper gives no numerical value at d = 2 and says the argument is weaker than Vitali for d ≤ 13, so it does not establish a new value or bound for F(Q²).
events.remains: F(Q²) = Γ_2 is unchanged: exact value open, and the bounds 1/λ_square ≈ 0.1179 and 1/4 − 1/384 are not improved by this paper. The D6 claim concerns general d.
events.direction: Lower-bound direction, for the cube problem in high dimensions. For d = 2 it does not move the constant.

events.what_happened: Gian Maria Dall'Ara and Adrian Dumitrescu, 'Rado's covering problem for cubes and balls: a semi-survey' (arXiv:2604.17509; v1 19 April 2026, v2 24 April 2026). A survey, not a new square result. For squares it: recounts Radó's 1928 problem and conjecture; attributes the two-dimensional disproof to Ajtai (1973) with F(Q²) < 1/4; gives F(Q²) ≤ 1/4 − 1/384 and F(Q²) ≥ 1/λ_square with λ_square = 8.4797… (Bereg–Dumitrescu–Jiang); states that no reasonable conjecture has emerged for F(Q²); and lists 'Can this be improved?' for both bounds as open problems. Its results on cubes and balls concern high dimensions; I did not read them in detail. Footnote 11 says the authors used Wolfram Alpha for a numerical minimum in the ball case (Section 6), which is computer algebra, not an AI system, and does not concern squares. Read through a summarising fetch of the arXiv HTML, with 125-character quote limits.
events.delivers: No new bound for squares. It restates the state of the art: 1/λ_square ≈ 0.1179 ≤ F(Q²) ≤ 1/4 − 1/384 (attributed to BDJ), and F(Q²) < 1/4 (Ajtai).
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: the exact value and both bounds, which it lists as open.

checked_by.qualification: Expert survey authors. Dumitrescu is the second named author of the BDJ paper whose bounds they report, and Dall'Ara wrote the 2025 cube paper, so they are not independent of the results they digest
checked_by.what_they_did: Digested the literature and restated the square bounds as the current state of the art, listing their improvement as open

events.direction: None for squares: it reports the square case as open with the bounds unchanged.

events.what_happened: Chengfei Xie and Gennian Ge, 'On the weighted hard-core model and Rado's covering problem for congruent Euclidean balls' (arXiv:2608.09744, math.MG; v1 10 August 2026, v2 25 August 2026). Definition 1.2 defines f(K) over translates of a symmetric convex body K, i.e. equal-size copies, and proves f(K) ≥ 2/(3^d + 2^d) for all symmetric convex K (improving the Vitali bound 3^-d). For the unit Euclidean ball it proves f(B^d) ≥ (log(3/(1+√3)) − O(log d/d))·d·3^-d for sufficiently large d. Its introduction restates Radó's F(Q²) ≥ 1/9 and conjecture 1/4, and Ajtai's F(Q²) < 1/4; the intro sentences I saw do not mention the BDJ lower bound of about 0.1179. Read through the abstract and a summarising fetch of the HTML; not quoted verbatim.
events.delivers: For equal-size (translate) copies of a symmetric convex body in dimension d: a guaranteed fraction 2/(3^d + 2^d). For d = 2 and K a square this formula gives 2/13 ≈ 0.154; that figure is my arithmetic from the formula, not a value the paper is quoted as stating for squares. For unit balls: an improvement for large d. Nothing here treats families of unequal squares.
events.remains: The bullet's problem: families of squares of unequal sizes, the exact value of F(Q²), and both square bounds.
events.direction: Lower-bound direction for the equal-size question and for balls. It does not move F(Q²) for mixed sizes, and its stated definition excludes them.

disputes.summary: Equal-square 1/4 result: Wikipedia credits A. Sokolin (1940), R. Rado and V. A. Zalgaller (1960) with proving the conjecture for equal squares; the 2026 survey describes Sokolin as generalising Radó's conjecture to F(Q^d) = 2^-d, i.e. stating a conjecture. Not resolved here; primary papers not read.

Radó's planar question is dated to a 1927 letter to Sierpiński by Dall'Ara (2025) and the 2026 survey, and to the 1928 publication by Wikipedia and the Xie–Ge introduction. I date the event to the 1928 public written argument.

summary: I ran 39 searches (listed below) and opened: the Wikipedia article and its raw wikitext, both read through a summarising fetch so quotes are not verbatim; the arXiv abstracts and HTML for Brass et al. 2008 (0804.1173), Xie–Ge 2026 (2608.09744), Dall'Ara 2025 (2510.06817) and the Dall'Ara–Dumitrescu semi-survey 2026 (2604.17509); the MARDI record for BDJ and Dumitrescu's 2014 Bridges exhibit page; and two arXiv items that proved to be dead ends. Nothing dated after 26 January 2024 changes the square-case bounds. The state of the art given by the April 2026 survey, which a BDJ co-author co-wrote, is 1/λ_square ≈ 0.1179 ≤ F(Q²) ≤ 1/4 − 1/384 = 95/384 ≈ 0.2474, with F(Q²) < 1/4 since Ajtai (1973); the survey lists improving both bounds as open. The in-window items are: Dall'Ara 2025, a Γ_d asymptotic for axis-parallel cubes in every dimension, which gives no d = 2 value and whose own text says its argument is weaker than Vitali for d ≤ 13; the survey, which restates; and Xie–Ge 2026, which treats equal-size translates of symmetric convex bodies and balls. Its Definition 1.2 is over translates, so it does not address the bullet's mixed-size squares. Close calls: (1) Xie–Ge's formula 2/(3^d + 2^d) gives 2/13 ≈ 0.154 at d = 2 for a square, above the BDJ lower bound of 0.1179. That would move the square bound only if it applied to families of unequal squares, and the stated definition restricts it to translates. I computed 2/13 from the formula. (2) Equal squares: Wikipedia credits Sokolin, R. Rado and Zalgaller with the 1/4 for equal squares; the survey describes Sokolin as conjecturing F(Q^d) = 2^-d. I record both and have not resolved the conflict. (3) The Xie–Ge introduction quotes the lower bound 1/9 and does not mention the BDJ bound of about 0.1179 that both Wikipedia and the survey give. Either the introduction is out of date or it omits the citation; unresolved. (4) The 1/4 − 1/1728 figure for Ajtai comes only from Wikipedia; the survey gives F(Q²) < 1/4 without a number. (5) Survey footnote 7 says that with two square sizes a fraction 1/8 can easily be covered, and cites Mirsky for 8/63. My reading is that these are guarantees for two-size families rather than upper bounds, but the primary text was not available in full and this remains unresolved. (6) The survey writes the BDJ upper bound as f(Q²) in one place and F(Q²) elsewhere; notation only. AI: I ran eight AI-targeted searches (AI proof and counterexample, AlphaEvolve and GPT, OpenAI, DeepMind and Anthropic, Claude, GPT-5.5, Gemini Deep Think and AlphaProof, AI computer search, Lean and Mathlib formalisation, and AI-generated proof claims). None attributes any step on this problem to an AI system, and no event credits one. The survey names Wolfram Alpha for a ball-case numerical computation (footnote 11). That is computer algebra, not AI, and does not concern squares; ai.none_found is therefore false for that event with an empty systems list. Other in-window AI-related papers concern other problems: arXiv 2609.15876 (Claude used for numerical routines on covering a square of side n+ε by n²+1 unit squares), arXiv 2511.02864 (AlphaEvolve, square packing), and arXiv 2512.19287 (GPT-5 on IMO 2025 Problem 6). I saw these only in search results, except that 2609.15876 is described from its search summary. None bears on this problem, so they are recorded as dead ends, not events.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the window as containing a move: Xie–Ge's f(K) ≥ 2/(3^d + 2^d) gives 2/13 ≈ 0.154 at d = 2 for a square, which exceeds the 0.1179 lower bound. This needs the translates restriction in Definition 1.2 to be dropped, and the paper does not allow that. A second reading: Dall'Ara's Theorem 1.3 holds for all d, including d = 2, and so could be read as improving F(Q²). It is an asymptotic statement with no value at d = 2, and the paper says its argument is weaker than Vitali for d ≤ 13, so it does not move the planar constant. A third reading: the 1/9 in the Xie–Ge introduction could be taken as the current lower bound. The survey and Wikipedia both give 1/λ_square ≈ 0.1179, which supersedes 1/9. The survey's 1/8 and 8/63 remarks (footnote 7) could also be read as upper bounds for two-size families, which would beat the record upper bound by a wide margin; I think the more likely reading is that they are guarantees, but the primary text would be needed to be sure.
what_would_settle_it: The primary texts: Ajtai (1973) for the 1/4 − 1/1728 construction; the BDJ SWAT 2008 paper and Algorithmica 57(3) 538–561 (DOI 10.1007/s00453-009-9298-z) for the 1/λ_square ≈ 0.1179 lower bound and the 1/4 − 1/384 construction. Also the survey's Section 5 and footnote 7 (what the 1/8 and 8/63 figures are) and Fig. 1, and whether the survey cites Dall'Ara 2025 and what Section 4 says about it. For Xie–Ge: the full introduction and reference list (whether it cites BDJ or the survey, and whether anywhere it applies f(K) to families of unequal squares). For the equal-square attribution: Sokolin (1940) and Zalgaller (1960). Finally, any arXiv paper after 10 August 2026 whose abstract names the square constant F(Q²).

events.credibility_reason: Attribution conflict: the 2026 survey describes Sokolin's 1940 contribution as a conjecture, not a proof; primary papers not read. The equal-square result itself is not disputed.

judgement.why: The statement asks for the value of F(Q²) for mixed-size squares, so every pre-snapshot result on it (Radó's 1/9, Ajtai's <1/4, BDJ's 0.1179 and 1/4−1/384) moves a bound rather than settling the value. Ajtai's family refutes Radó's 1/4 conjecture, but the statement asks for the value and does not assert 1/4, so I scored it as a bound with null object role. Equal squares is a restriction of the statement, so it is a case. Of the in-window items: Dall'Ara 2025 is an all-dimension asymptotic that by its own account gives nothing at d=2, so it is none for this problem. The survey only restates results (none). Xie–Ge restricts to translates (equal sizes), which changes the question, so it is a variant; the 2/13 is the researcher's arithmetic and in any case applies only to equal squares. No AI system did any of the mathematics. Wolfram Alpha in the survey is computer algebra.
judgement.doubts: The survey's footnote 7 (1/8 for two sizes, Mirsky's 8/63) remains unresolved; read as upper bounds, those figures would contradict the stated record. I take them to be guarantees, as the researcher does. Ajtai's 1/4−1/1728 figure rests only on Wikipedia.
